beginner: Apple trees grow best in deep, rich soil that drains well, the kind of loamy soil that holds some moisture but never stays soggy. The one rule that matters most: the spot must drain. Apple roots rot if water sits around them, and that is the fastest way to lose a young tree. If your soil is heavy clay or stays wet, plant the tree on a low mound of soil instead of digging a deep hole, so water drains away from the roots.
seasoned: Apple wants a deep, well-drained loam with steady moisture and moderate organic matter. The non-negotiable is drainage: apple roots will not tolerate standing water, and wet feet drive crown and root rots that kill young trees faster than any pest. On heavy clay or a high water table, plant on a raised berm or mound rather than amending the planting hole, which only makes a sump. Match the rootstock to the site as well, M9 and M26 dislike wet ground more than the more vigorous stocks do.

beginner: Apple trees like soil that is slightly acidic, a pH around 6.0 to 6.5 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline soil is, where 7.0 is neutral). Test your soil before you plant, since it is much easier to fix the pH now than after the tree is in the ground. If the test says your soil is too acidic, garden lime raises the pH; if it is too alkaline, garden sulfur lowers it. Your local extension office can test a soil sample for you.
seasoned: Apple does best at a slightly acidic pH of about 6.0 to 6.5, and tolerates roughly 5.5 to 7.0. Test the soil before planting and adjust the whole root zone, not just the hole, because correcting pH around an established tree is slow. Lime raises a low pH; elemental sulfur lowers a high one. Outside this band, iron and manganese become less available and you see interveinal yellowing on new growth even when those nutrients are present.

beginner: Feed apple trees once a year, in early spring before the buds open, with a balanced fertilizer. Go easy: too much feeding makes lots of soft leaves instead of fruit and invites a serious disease called fire blight. If the tree is growing well and putting out healthy new branches each year, it may not need much at all.
seasoned: Fertilize lightly in early spring before bud break, guided by shoot growth: a healthy young apple makes about 12 to 18 inches of new shoot growth per year, so feed to reach that, not beyond. Excess nitrogen drives soft, leafy growth that is highly susceptible to fire blight and delays fruiting. Mature trees on fertile soil often need little or no nitrogen.

beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. A balanced one like 10-10-10 is fine for apples. The first number (nitrogen) is the one to keep modest, too much makes the tree grow leaves instead of apples.
seasoned: A balanced N-P-K ratio (the three numbers on the bag, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium), such as 10-10-10, applied at a modest rate; lean toward lower nitrogen on vigorous trees to limit fire-blight-prone growth.

beginner: A simple guideline is a small amount that grows with the tree's age, following the directions on the fertilizer bag. When in doubt, use less, an underfed apple tree is healthier than an overfed one.
seasoned: A common home rule is about 1/8 lb of actual nitrogen per year of tree age, capped near 1 lb actual N for a mature tree; always follow the product label and adjust down if annual shoot growth is already strong.

beginner: Apples do not pair with other plants the way vegetables do. For an apple, the neighbor that counts is a second, different apple variety planted within about 50 ft that blooms at the same time, because most apple trees need another apple nearby to make fruit. Right around the trunk, do the opposite of planting companions: keep grass and other plants away from the base, out to the edge of the branches, because they steal water and food from the young tree. Use mulch there instead, and never plant an apple near a black walnut tree, which poisons the soil for apples.
seasoned: Apple does not companion-plant in the vegetable sense; the interactions that actually matter are pollination and root competition. The single most important neighbor is a second, bloom-overlapping apple variety (the pollinizer) within about 50 ft, because nearly all apples are self-unfruitful. At the trunk, the rule is the reverse of companionship: keep turf and aggressive perennials out of the root zone, since grass competes hard with a young tree for water and nitrogen. Maintain a mulched, vegetation-free circle out to the dripline, and avoid siting near black walnut, whose juglone is toxic to apple.

beginner: Plant a ring of daffodils around your apple tree, out where the branches reach. They come up early in spring with cheerful flowers, help keep grass from creeping in toward the trunk, and because they are poisonous to nibble, they discourage mice and deer. They die back in summer, so they stay out of the tree's way.
seasoned: A ring of daffodils at the drip line is a traditional apple-guild move with two intended jobs: the early foliage and bulbs form a band that helps hold back creeping grass, the tree's main competitor, and daffodils are toxic enough that voles and deer tend to avoid grazing through them to the trunk. They emerge and feed before the canopy leafs out, then go dormant, so they do not compete with the tree in summer. Treat this as a useful cultural barrier rather than a measured yield booster.

beginner: Comfrey is a leafy plant that grows well around apple trees. Its roots reach deep down, so it does not steal water from the tree, and it crowds out grass. A few times each summer you can cut the big leaves and lay them on the soil under the tree, where they rot down into natural food for it. Its flowers also bring in helpful bees.
seasoned: Comfrey is a workhorse of the apple guild. Its deep taproot pulls from well below the tree's surface feeder roots, so it does not compete for the same water and nutrients, and it shades out grass along the row. Chopped two or three times a season and dropped under the tree, its lush leaves break down into a mineral-rich mulch, and the flowers feed pollinators and beneficials. The dynamic-accumulator framing is more tradition than proven chemistry, but the practical value as non-competing mulch and grass suppression is real.

beginner: White clover is a low, soft plant you can grow as a living carpet under your apple tree. It pulls nitrogen from the air and feeds it into the soil for the tree, while covering the ground to keep weeds down and hold in moisture. It is tough enough to walk on at picking time. Just keep it from growing right against the trunk.
seasoned: Dutch white clover makes a strong living mulch under apples. As a legume it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through its root symbiosis, feeding the tree slowly while staying low and tolerating the foot traffic of harvest. It covers the ground to suppress weeds and hold moisture without the aggressive grass competition that bare turf brings. Keep it back from the immediate trunk zone, and note it does draw some moisture, so on dry sites manage it accordingly.

beginner: Keep apple trees far away from black walnut trees. Black walnuts release a natural chemical called juglone from their roots and leaves that is poisonous to apple trees and can make them sicken and die. The chemical spreads through the soil well past the walnut's branches, so give them a very wide berth, at least 50 feet from a big walnut.
seasoned: Black walnut is a definitive bad neighbor for apple. Its roots, hulls, and leaf litter release juglone, an allelopathic compound that is toxic to a wide range of sensitive plants, and apple is among those affected, showing decline and dieback within the walnut's root zone. The effect extends well beyond the visible canopy, roughly to the full root spread (commonly cited at fifty-plus feet from a mature tree), so siting matters more than spacing tweaks: keep apples entirely out of a black walnut's root zone.

beginner: Do not let lawn grass grow right up against your apple tree's trunk. The grass competes with the young tree for water and food, and trees with grass to the trunk grow slower and start fruiting later. Grass at the trunk also hides mice that can chew the bark in winter. Keep a clear or mulched circle about two feet around the trunk, with the mulch pulled back slightly so it does not touch the bark.
seasoned: Letting turfgrass grow right up to an apple trunk is a quiet but real drag on the tree, especially when young. Grass competes directly for water and nitrogen in the surface zone where the tree's feeder roots sit, and a documented extension experiment showed grass against apple trunks delayed the onset of fruiting and reduced vegetative growth versus a kept-clear area. There is a second hazard: dense grass and mulch against the trunk harbor voles that girdle bark over winter. Maintain a vegetation-free or mulched strip about two feet out from the trunk (mulch pulled back a few inches off the bark itself).

beginner: This is the classic "worm in the apple." You find a small hole in the apple with brown crumbly stuff (frass) around it, and a tunnel into the core when you cut it open. Bad apples drop early.
seasoned: Larvae tunnel into the fruit core, leaving a frass-filled entry hole (often at the calyx end) and brown trails; infested apples drop early or are inedible.

beginner: A small moth lays eggs on the tiny apples in spring; the eggs hatch into caterpillars that crawl into the fruit. There can be two batches a summer, so the problem repeats.
seasoned: Cydia pomonella; female moths lay eggs on developing fruit and young leaves near bloom, and hatching larvae bore into the apple. Two or more generations per season in most regions.

beginner: Keep the ground under the tree clean of fallen apples, and wrap a band of cardboard around the trunk to trap crawling caterpillars. Nearby neglected apple trees make it worse.
seasoned: Orchard sanitation (clear dropped fruit and debris), keep nearby abandoned apple trees pruned or removed, and band trunks to catch larvae seeking pupation sites.

beginner: Start here: pick up and destroy every apple that drops, do not leave them under the tree, since the caterpillars ride out in the fallen fruit. This step alone lowers next year's moths.
seasoned: Removing and destroying dropped and infested fruit through the season strips out larvae before they exit to pupate; the backbone every other step builds on.

beginner: Hang a scented (pheromone) trap to tell you when the moths are flying, so you know the right moment to bag fruit or spray. The trap is a timing tool, not a cure on its own.
seasoned: Wing traps baited with sex pheromone time the other steps to egg hatch; UC IPM notes trapping alone is not a reliable way to reduce damage on an isolated tree.

beginner: Slip a paper bag or nylon footie over each young apple about a month after bloom and staple it shut. It is the most effective spray-free option, worth the effort on a small tree.
seasoned: Bagging at 1/2 to 1 inch fruit excludes egg-laying moths; UC IPM calls it the only nonchemical method effective enough to use alone, even under heavy pressure.

beginner: A white clay film sprayed on the tree makes it an unpleasant place for moths to lay eggs. It only partly controls codling moth, so reapply through the season and expect to pair it with the steps above.
seasoned: Kaolin gives only fair to moderate codling moth control and washes off, so keep new growth covered; heavy use can flare European red mites or scale.

beginner: If the steps above are not holding, spinosad is a strong organic spray, but it only works if timed to when the eggs hatch, which is what the trap tells you. It is hard on bees while wet, so spray at dusk and never on open blossoms.
seasoned: Spinosad, timed to egg hatch on a petal-fall or degree-day schedule, controls the boring larvae; toxic to bees while wet, so apply at dusk away from bloom.

beginner: Only for a heavy infestation nothing else has held. A synthetic that kills fast but hits bees, fish, and the good bugs too, so it is a last resort, not a routine spray.
seasoned: A broad-spectrum contact pyrethroid is rescue-only; it sets back natural enemies and can trigger mite or aphid resurgence. Observe the label pre-harvest interval.

beginner: The apple skin gets little dimples and the inside has brown squiggly trails. Unlike the codling moth's single tunnel to the core, this is a maze of trails through the flesh.
seasoned: Adult flies lay eggs under the skin; larvae tunnel through the flesh leaving dimpled, pitted fruit with brown winding trails inside.

beginner: A fly pokes the apple skin in summer and lays eggs just underneath, and the maggots eat through the apple.
seasoned: Rhagoletis pomonella; flies emerge in summer and sting the fruit surface to lay eggs just under the skin.

beginner: Picking up fallen apples quickly stops the next generation. Bagging the fruit also keeps the flies out.
seasoned: Sanitation (remove drops within a few days, before larvae exit into the soil) breaks the cycle; bagging fruit excludes the flies.

beginner: Start here: pick up fallen apples every few days, before the maggots crawl out into the soil to overwinter. Clearing the drops promptly breaks the cycle.
seasoned: Removing drops within a few days, before larvae exit into the soil, is the foundational step against apple maggot.

beginner: Hang sticky red ball traps that look like ripe apples; the flies land to lay eggs and get stuck. Use about one trap per 100 to 150 apples on the tree, and get them up by mid-June before egg-laying starts.
seasoned: Baited red spheres at roughly one per 100 to 150 fruit trap out egg-laying females and can control apple maggot in a small planting, not just monitor it; keep them sticky and serviced.

beginner: Bagging young apples keeps the flies off the fruit entirely, the surest spray-free option where you have the patience to bag each one.
seasoned: Paper bags applied at 1/2 to 1 inch fruit exclude apple maggot as well as codling moth for the rest of the season.

beginner: A white clay film repels apple maggot flies and gives strong control of this pest, though it must be reapplied and washed off the fruit at harvest.
seasoned: Kaolin gives strong control of apple maggot specifically; keep the film renewed on new growth through the egg-laying period.

beginner: If traps and clay are not enough, a spinosad spray helps, but it is hard on bees while wet, so spray at dusk and not on open flowers.
seasoned: Spinosad, applied when flies are active, backs up trapping; toxic to bees while wet, so time it to dusk.

beginner: A last resort for heavy pressure only. It works fast but kills bees, fish, and beneficial insects, so keep it off flowers and out of water.
seasoned: Rescue-only; broad-spectrum and disruptive to natural enemies, with a label pre-harvest interval to observe.

beginner: Look for little crescent or D-shaped scars on the small green apples in spring. Damaged fruit often drops while still small.
seasoned: Crescent-shaped (D-shaped) scars on young fruit from egg-laying; larvae feed inside, causing misshapen fruit and early drop.

beginner: A tiny beetle (weevil) that scars the baby apples right after the flowers drop their petals.
seasoned: Conotrachelus nenuphar; a small weevil that attacks young fruit shortly after petal fall.

beginner: Clean up dropped apples promptly, they carry the next generation.
seasoned: Prompt removal of dropped fruit (which carries larvae) and good sanitation reduce next-year pressure.

beginner: Start here: clean up dropped apples promptly, since they carry the grubs, and on cool early mornings you can spread a sheet under the tree and tap the branches to jar the beetles down and collect them.
seasoned: Prompt removal of dropped fruit lowers next year's weevils; jarring adults onto a sheet at first light, when they are sluggish, physically removes them.

beginner: A white clay film applied right after the petals fall, when the weevils attack the young fruit, deters them from feeding and laying eggs. Reapply through the season to keep new fruit covered.
seasoned: Kaolin gives fair to moderate plum curculio control; start at petal fall, the critical window, and reapply as fruit expands and the film washes off.

beginner: Only if clay is not holding and the weevils are ruining the crop. If you spray, the timing that matters is just after the blossoms drop their petals, and again about two weeks later. This is a synthetic that hits bees and beneficials, so keep it off open flowers and treat it as a last resort.
seasoned: A rescue-only conventional; time it to petal fall and a follow-up about two weeks later, after bloom so bees are off the flowers. Broad-spectrum and disruptive to natural enemies, with a label pre-harvest interval.

beginner: Fluffy white cottony patches show up on branches and around pruning cuts, it looks like bits of cotton wool stuck to the bark.
seasoned: White, cottony tufts on shoots, pruning wounds, and roots; heavy colonies cause galls and weaken young trees.

beginner: A small aphid that covers itself in white waxy fluff while it feeds on the bark and roots.
seasoned: Eriosoma lanigerum; colonies feed on bark and roots, secreting the protective waxy wool.

beginner: Some rootstocks (MM106, MM111) naturally resist this pest, a good reason to ask which rootstock your tree is on.
seasoned: Choosing a resistant rootstock (MM106, MM111 resist woolly apple aphid) avoids the worst root colonies.

beginner: The best defense is the rootstock your tree is grafted on: MM106 and MM111 rootstocks resist woolly apple aphid, so ask which one your tree is on when you buy.
seasoned: Woolly apple aphid resistant rootstocks (MM106, MM111) avoid the worst root colonies; the highest-leverage, plant-once choice.

beginner: A strong jet of water knocks the cottony colonies off shoots and pruning wounds, and cutting off badly infested twigs removes the worst of them. Both are cheap first steps before any spray.
seasoned: A forceful spray dislodges the woolly colonies on sturdy wood; prune out heavily infested wood to remove established galls, and repeat as colonies rebuild.

beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps feed on woolly apple aphid and often keep it in check on their own, so protect them by avoiding broad sprays.
seasoned: Conserving resident natural enemies usually keeps woolly apple aphid down; broad-spectrum sprays that wipe them out are what let it flare, so the softer this ladder stays, the better.

beginner: For stubborn colonies, spray them directly with insecticidal soap. It only kills what it wets, so hit the cottony patches thoroughly, and it spares beneficials once dry.
seasoned: Contact soap smothers the exposed colonies but does not reach the wax-protected or root-feeding aphids, so it gives only partial control; coverage and repeat sprays matter.

beginner: Horticultural oil smothers the aphids and has a bit more staying power than soap. Do not spray it in heat above 90°F or on a drought-stressed tree, and keep it away from a recent sulfur spray.
seasoned: Narrow-range oil gives partial control by smothering; the waxy wool shields some aphids, so thorough coverage is key. Avoid oil on stressed trees, above 90°F, or within 2 weeks of sulfur. There is no conventional rung here, since pyrethroids destroy this aphid's natural enemies and make outbreaks worse.

beginner: Dark, fuzzy olive-green spots appear on the leaves, and the apples get rough, scabby, cracked patches. In a bad year the tree drops its leaves early.
seasoned: Olive-green to brown, velvety spots on leaves that later turn dark and corky; scabby, cracked lesions on fruit. Severe infection causes leaf yellowing and early defoliation.

beginner: A fungus that survives winter in last year's fallen leaves and spreads in cool, wet spring weather onto the new leaves and fruit.
seasoned: Venturia inaequalis; spores overwinter in fallen leaves and infect during wet spring weather, with infection periods driven by leaf wetness and temperature.

beginner: The single best move is to rake up and remove fallen leaves every autumn, that is where the fungus hides over winter. Better yet, plant a scab-resistant variety like Liberty so you rarely have to spray.
seasoned: Rake and remove fallen leaves in autumn (destroys the overwintering source), prune for airflow, and plant scab-resistant varieties such as Liberty.

beginner: The surest fix is to plant a scab-resistant apple like Liberty, so you rarely have to spray at all.
seasoned: Scab-resistant cultivars such as Liberty remove most of the spray schedule; the highest-leverage control for a disease that is hard to cure once it is going.

beginner: Rake up and remove every fallen leaf in autumn. The fungus overwinters in last year's leaves, so clearing them is the single best thing you can do after variety choice.
seasoned: Removing and destroying fallen leaves in autumn strips out the overwintering source, lowering next spring's spore load.

beginner: Prune the tree so air moves through it and the leaves dry fast after rain. Scab needs long wet periods to infect, so a drier canopy gets less disease.
seasoned: Opening the canopy shortens leaf-wetness periods, denying the fungus the sustained moisture it needs to infect.

beginner: If you grow a susceptible variety, sulfur is the organic spray, but it must go on in spring before infection, on a protective schedule. Once the spots are everywhere it is too late for that year, so prevention is the game. Do not spray sulfur in heat above 90°F, since it burns leaves.
seasoned: Sulfur is a protectant only, so time it to spring infection periods and reapply; it will not cure established scab. Avoid it above 90°F and within 2 weeks of an oil spray, and note it can harm predatory mites.

beginner: Branch tips and flower clusters suddenly turn black and look burned, as if scorched by fire, and the tip bends over into a hook shape. It can kill whole branches or the tree.
seasoned: Blossoms and shoot tips suddenly wilt, blacken, and die, bending into a characteristic "shepherd's crook"; affected branches look scorched. Sunken, oozing cankers form on wood.

beginner: Bacteria that infect through the flowers in warm, wet spring weather. Fast, soft growth from too much fertilizer makes it much worse.
seasoned: Erwinia amylovora; bacteria infect through blossoms and wounds in warm, wet spring weather and spread fastest on lush, nitrogen-pushed growth.

beginner: Go easy on fertilizer, soft sappy growth is what fire blight loves. Prune only in dry weather, and choose varieties known to resist it where this disease is common.
seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen (soft growth is most susceptible), plant less-susceptible varieties and rootstocks, and prune in dry conditions. Forecast models guide bloom-time management.

beginner: Where fire blight is common, the most important choice is a less-susceptible variety and rootstock. There is no spray that cures this disease, so start by not planting the ones that get it worst.
seasoned: Variety and rootstock susceptibility varies widely; choosing resistant stock is the highest-leverage control for a bacterial disease with no cure.

beginner: Go easy on fertilizer: soft, sappy new growth from too much nitrogen is exactly what fire blight races through, so feed sparingly. Clean up and destroy any blighted prunings rather than leaving them near the tree.
seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which pushes the succulent growth fire blight colonizes fastest, and destroy infected prunings; there is no cure once the bacteria are in the wood.

beginner: This is the main control: cut off each blackened, hooked shoot about a hand's length (6 to 8 inches) below the damage, into healthy wood, and destroy it. Do it in dry weather, and dip your pruners in a bleach solution between cuts so you do not spread it.
seasoned: Cut 6 to 8 inches beyond the visible margin into healthy wood, ideally in dry or dormant weather; placing the cut far enough below the strike matters more than tool sterilizing, though dipping shears in 10% bleach is still wise.

beginner: A copper spray at bloom can slow new blossom infections, but it is a limited, preventive help, not a cure, and it cannot save wood that is already infected. Copper is toxic to fish and builds up in the soil, so use it sparingly and follow the label.
seasoned: Fixed copper at early bloom reduces new blossom infection but does not cure existing strikes; a limited protectant, not a fix. Copper accumulates in soil and is toxic to aquatic life, so limit repeat use over the years.

beginner: Vivid yellow-orange spots appear on the tops of the leaves a few weeks after the tree blooms, and sometimes on the fruit. They are hard to miss because the color is so bright.
seasoned: Bright yellow-orange spots on upper leaf surfaces (sometimes with small black dots) appearing shortly after bloom, and orange lesions on fruit; heavy infection causes early leaf drop.

beginner: An unusual fungus that lives part of its life on apple and part on nearby cedar or juniper trees. It bounces between the two, so apples near cedars get it.
seasoned: Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae; the fungus needs two hosts, alternating between apple and nearby red cedar or juniper, releasing spores from cedar galls in spring rains.

beginner: This disease needs a cedar or juniper tree nearby to survive. Removing those within a few hundred feet, or planting a rust-resistant apple variety, breaks the cycle.
seasoned: Remove red cedar or juniper within a few hundred feet if practical, or choose rust-resistant apple varieties; the disease cannot complete its cycle without the cedar host.

beginner: Rust needs a nearby cedar or juniper to survive, so two things break its cycle: plant a rust-resistant apple variety, or remove cedars and junipers within a few hundred feet if you can.
seasoned: Rust-resistant cultivars, or eliminating the alternate juniper host within a few hundred feet, break the two-host cycle; on light infections the damage is mostly cosmetic.

beginner: Rake up fallen infected leaves and pick off the bright orange-spotted ones. On most trees rust is more unsightly than harmful, so this and variety choice are usually enough.
seasoned: Removing infected leaves lowers local inoculum; on a healthy tree light rust is largely cosmetic and rarely warrants spraying.

beginner: Only if your tree gets heavy rust every year. A protectant like sulfur must go on in spring, starting around when the buds show pink, before the spots appear; it cannot clear rust that is already there. Do not spray sulfur in heat above 90°F.
seasoned: Sulfur is a preventive protectant applied from pink-bud through early fruit set where rust has a history; it is weaker on rust than synthetic options and will not cure existing lesions, so most gardeners never need it. Avoid it above 90°F and near an oil spray.

beginner: A white powdery coating, like flour dusted on the leaves and new shoots. Affected tips grow poorly and the leaves curl.
seasoned: White, felt-like fungal growth on leaves, shoots, and buds; infected shoots are stunted and leaves curl. Fruit may develop a russeted netting.

beginner: A fungus that hides in the buds over winter and spreads in warm, humid spring weather onto the new growth.
seasoned: Podosphaera leucotricha; overwinters in buds and spreads in spring, favored by warm days and humid nights (it does not need leaf wetness).

beginner: Prune the tree so air moves through it, mildew hates dry, breezy conditions, and cut out any white-coated twigs in winter.
seasoned: Prune for good air circulation, choose less-susceptible varieties, and remove infected wood during dormant pruning.

beginner: If mildew is a yearly problem, choose a less-susceptible variety; it is the easiest long-term fix.
seasoned: Cultivar susceptibility varies; choosing a less-susceptible variety is the lowest-effort durable control.

beginner: Prune the tree open so air moves through it. Powdery mildew hates dry, breezy conditions, so good airflow makes a big difference.
seasoned: Opening the canopy for air movement suppresses mildew, which favors humid, still air; unlike scab it does not need leaf wetness to infect.

beginner: Snip off the white-coated shoots as you see them, and cut out any infected twigs during winter pruning. Go easy on nitrogen, since soft new growth is what mildew colonizes.
seasoned: Prune out white-coated shoots and infected wood at dormant pruning, and avoid nitrogen-pushed flushes of the tender growth mildew prefers.

beginner: If mildew keeps coming back, sulfur is the classic organic spray, applied before it takes hold. Do not use it in heat above 90°F, since it burns leaves.
seasoned: Sulfur is a reliable protectant fungicide and miticide for powdery mildew; apply preventively where it recurs, avoid above 90°F and within 2 weeks of oil, and note it can set back predatory mites.

beginner: Water deeply but not too often, aim for about 1 inch of water a week while the tree is growing and making fruit. Water more in hot, dry spells and less once the leaves drop in fall.
seasoned: Deep, infrequent irrigation: about 1 inch of water per week through the growing season, more in heat and during fruit sizing, tapering off as the tree goes dormant.

beginner: About 1 inch a week. The easiest way is one long, slow soak that gets the water down deep to the roots, rather than a quick daily sprinkle.
seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week as a baseline (a deep soak that wets the full root zone), increasing during fruit sizing in mid to late summer.

beginner: Use a soaker hose or drip line, or just let a hose trickle slowly at the edge of the branches. Keep water off the trunk itself, and spread mulch around the tree (but not touching the trunk) to hold moisture in.
seasoned: Drip or a slow soak at the dripline; keep water off the trunk and crown to avoid collar rot, and mulch to hold moisture (pulled back a few inches from the trunk).

beginner: If the leaves yellow and the ground stays soggy, the tree is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly. Rot at the base of the trunk is a warning sign.
seasoned: Yellowing leaves, waterlogged or persistently soggy soil, and root or collar rot at the trunk base signal too much water or poor drainage.

beginner: Wilting or dry, brown leaf edges, and small fruit that drops early, mean the tree is too dry, especially in mid to late summer when the apples are sizing up.
seasoned: Wilting or scorched leaf margins, premature fruit drop, and small fruit in summer indicate drought stress, especially during fruit sizing.

beginner: First-year tree: give it a deep soak once or twice a week all summer so the roots get established. Do not let it dry out.
seasoned: Establishment: deep-soak 1 to 2 times per week through the first summer to drive root growth; do not let the root ball dry out.

beginner: While the apples are growing bigger, water once a week and keep it steady, this is when uneven watering causes problems.
seasoned: Fruit sizing: water weekly and consistently as apples bulk up; even moisture now prevents bitter pit and cracking.

beginner: In winter, when the tree is bare and resting, you barely need to water at all, rain usually covers it.
seasoned: Dormant: minimal irrigation; rely on natural precipitation unless soils are unusually dry over a mild winter.

beginner: Steady, even watering matters most in the first year and while the apples are growing. Big swings between bone-dry and soaked can cause fruit problems.
seasoned: Consistent soil moisture during fruit sizing prevents bitter pit and cracking; a young tree in its establishment year needs the most attention to even watering.

beginner: Two times matter most for watering: the first year after planting, and mid-to-late summer when the apples are filling out. In winter the tree needs almost no water.
seasoned: Establishment year (root development) and fruit sizing (mid to late summer) are the critical irrigation windows; dormant-season water needs are minimal.

beginner: This step does not apply to apples. Hardening off means slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to the outdoors, but you do not start an apple from seed indoors. You buy a young tree, either bare-root (no soil on the roots) or in a pot, and plant it straight into the ground, so there is nothing to harden off.
seasoned: Not applicable. Apple is planted as a bare-root dormant tree or a potted nursery tree, not started from seed indoors, so there is no tender seedling to harden off. Plant during dormancy (late winter to early spring) and the tree breaks bud already acclimated to outdoor conditions.

beginner: If your tree comes bare-root (bare roots, no pot), plant it in late winter or early spring while it is still leafless and dormant, as soon as you can dig the soil. Soak the roots in a bucket of water for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough that the roots can spread out without folding. The key thing: find the graft union (the bumpy spot low on the trunk where the top variety was joined to the roots) and keep it about 2 to 3 in above the soil, never bury it. Fill the hole with the same soil you dug out, water well, and tie small trees to a stake. A potted tree is planted the same way and can go in anytime through spring.
seasoned: Plant a bare-root tree while fully dormant, late winter to early spring, as soon as the ground is workable.
